# omada_wireless_network (Resource)

Manages a wireless network (SSID) on the Omada Controller.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Omitted radio/security settings use defaults only on creation.
# After import, omit them to preserve the observed settings.
# Keep passphrase configured for later secured updates.
# Changing wlan_group_id replaces the SSID; review connectivity and recreation settings.
resource "omada_wireless_network" "example" {
  site_id       = omada_site.example.id
  name          = "HomeWiFi"
  wlan_group_id = omada_wlan_group.default.id
  band          = 3 # Both 2.4GHz and 5GHz
  security      = 3 # WPA2/WPA3-Personal
  passphrase    = var.wifi_password
  broadcast     = true
  vlan_id       = 50
  enable_11r    = true # Fast BSS Transition (802.11r)
  pmf_mode      = 2    # Optional PMF
}

variable "wifi_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
```

## Existing SSIDs and migration

Creation defaults remain `band = 3`, `security = 3`, `broadcast = true`, `enable_11r = false`, and `pmf_mode = 2`. On an existing or imported SSID, omitting these attributes preserves the observed settings. Set them explicitly to enforce those values. Removing a configured attribute relinquishes control; it no longer resets that setting to its creation default.

Updates preserve supported writable controller settings outside the configured changes, including guest controls, schedule/filter associations, rate limits, multicast, PSK mode/encryption/rekey, MLO, and Wi-Fi sharing. The provider reads a fresh snapshot and stops before writing if required settings are incomplete or an unrecognized field could be lost. It currently supports updates to open (`0`) and WPA-Personal (`3`) SSIDs with default or bridge VLAN settings. Other security/VLAN modes require an expanded, verified API contract.

`vlan_id` is different: omission selects the default VLAN. Keep a custom VLAN explicitly configured after import. Changing a custom VLAN requires one matching controller network; failed, missing, or ambiguous lookups stop the operation.

### WLAN-group changes and replacement

Changing `wlan_group_id` replaces the SSID. The provider cannot move an existing SSID between groups. Terraform deletes using the old site/group/SSID identity and creates in the requested group, recording the new controller-returned ID. Changing `site_id` also continues to require replacement. Import IDs remain `site_id/wlan_group_id/ssid_id`; existing state needs no migration or re-import.

Omitting `wlan_group_id` on an existing or imported SSID retains its group, including during unrelated updates. Omission on initial creation uses the provider's existing default-group discovery. An explicitly configured group that is unknown during planning remains unknown and can conservatively require replacement even if it later resolves to the old group. Review the plan; resolve the group reference before applying if that replacement is unwanted.

Replacement can interrupt connectivity and discards unmanaged settings from the old SSID, including guest controls, schedules, filters, and rate limits. Preservation during ordinary updates does not carry those settings into a new object. Configure the desired radio/security/VLAN values and `passphrase` for secured recreation; omitted settings use creation defaults. Record controller-only settings before replacement and restore them separately as needed. Known invalid security/password combinations, including a secured replacement without `passphrase`, fail during planning before deletion. Values still unknown at plan time are checked when resolved during apply; resolve those dependencies first if a later error would leave an unacceptable interruption.

Terraform normally destroys before creating. If the new creation fails, the old SSID has already been removed; correct the error and apply again. `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` reverses the order, but requires the controller to permit both SSIDs to exist simultaneously. Duplicate-name, capacity, or group restrictions may prevent it; it does not guarantee uninterrupted connectivity. A rejected create leaves the old SSID managed. A rejected delete retains the old identity for retry. These failure cases are covered by synthetic controllers, with hardware behavior still to be verified.

### VLAN refresh and readback

The controller's selected VLAN mode determines `vlan_id`: default mode (`0`) reads as null, even if the response still contains a previous custom VLAN or an effective VLAN number. Custom mode (`1`) uses the bridge VLAN, falling back to a single valid `currentVlanId` when no bridge VLAN is supplied. VLAN IDs must be 1–4094.

A missing/null VLAN setting or mode, unsupported mode, invalid VLAN, or ambiguous fallback produces an error and preserves prior resource state. Such responses are not interpreted as a switch to the default VLAN. The `omada_wireless_networks` data source uses the same rules.

If the controller changes a managed SSID to the default VLAN, refresh clears the old custom value from state. A normal plan will then propose restoring an explicitly configured `vlan_id`; removing that configuration accepts the default VLAN and settles without another write. No re-import is needed.

Create and update validate VLAN readback. A different observed VLAN is saved with an error instead of reporting the requested value as applied. If an update returns uninterpretable VLAN data, prior state is retained. When readback returns a decoded SSID with an ID, that identity is retained on a VLAN mapping error so Terraform can clean it up. Transport, lookup, and JSON decoding failures before the resource receives that object retain the client's existing behavior. These behaviors are verified with synthetic controllers; hardware validation remains pending.

### Password ownership

Keep `passphrase` configured for secured creation and updates. Import and refresh never copy a controller-returned password into state: responses can contain plaintext, an omitted value, or an indistinguishable mask. Consequently, remote password drift is not detected. Supplying a password after import may write that password while preserving the other settings.

Removing `passphrase` does not open the network or clear its password. For an update that removes it, a previously configured key may be reused only when this provider has recorded its origin in private state after a successful create/update. The resulting state removes the key; a later secured update requires `passphrase` again. Old state without that marker is untrusted, even if it contains a nonempty key. Keep the real password configured through a successful update before relying on removal behavior. An imported secured SSID without a configured key can be read, but a change requiring PATCH fails before mutation.

To open an SSID, explicitly set `security = 0` and remove `passphrase`. To secure it again, set `security = 3` and supply the password. Password-only changes preserve existing PSK version, encryption, and rekey settings; a new secured network starts with the provider's existing PSK defaults.

### Controller compatibility

The writable-field inventory combines TP-Link's [v5.9.9 Web API reference](https://community.tp-link.com/en/business/forum/topic/590430?moduleId=582) with this provider's existing v6 request model. Tests include synthetic controllers and an isolated Software Controller 6.1.0.19 run with the corresponding client/WLAN-discovery fixes integrated. That run covers secured SSID create/import/group replacement, rename, password rotation, default/custom VLAN transitions, and stable plans; it does not establish physical-device compatibility. Web API field names and PMF mode meanings vary by controller version. The 6.1 response summaries `vlanEnable` and top-level `vlanId`, plus create-only `deviceType`, are excluded from PATCH. Authoritative `vlanSetting` and the existing device target are preserved. Unknown fields, legacy VLAN payloads, and unsupported modes stop updates rather than being silently omitted. Open-network PMF defaults remain a known 6.1 compatibility issue. Verify payload acceptance and PMF behavior on your controller before relying on these changes in production.

## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) The SSID name (broadcast name).
- `site_id` (String) The ID of the site this resource belongs to.

### Optional

- `band` (Number) Radio band bitmask: 1=2.4GHz, 2=5GHz, 3=both. Defaults to 3 on creation; omission preserves existing settings.
- `broadcast` (Boolean) Whether the SSID is broadcast (visible). Set false for hidden networks. Defaults to true on creation; omission preserves existing settings.
- `enable_11r` (Boolean) Enable 802.11r Fast Roaming. Defaults to false on creation; omission preserves existing settings.
- `passphrase` (String, Sensitive) The Wi-Fi password (WPA pre-shared key). Required for secured creation and updates without a previously configured key, including imports. API-returned keys are not trusted. Removing this attribute does not clear the remote key; set security to 0 to open the network.
- `pmf_mode` (Number) Protected Management Frames mode: 1=disabled, 2=optional, 3=required. Defaults to 2 on creation; omission preserves existing settings. Verify mode meanings for your controller version.
- `security` (Number) Security mode: 0=Open, 3=WPA2/WPA3-Personal. Defaults to 3 on creation; omission preserves existing settings. Other modes are unsupported.
- `vlan_id` (Number) Custom VLAN ID to assign to this SSID. If not set, uses the default VLAN.
- `wlan_group_id` (String) The WLAN group ID. Omission uses the default group on creation and retains the current group on updates. Changing the group requires replacement.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) The unique identifier of the SSID.

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
# Import by site_id/wlan_group_id/ssid_id
terraform import omada_wireless_network.example site-id/wlan-group-id/ssid-id
```
